extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulemakers, federal regulators, and public commenters on Clean Water Act Section 401 rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Public-comment legal/technical critique of EPA's proposed revisions to Clean Water Act Section 401 regulations, arguing statutory interpretation, procedural, environmental, and consultation standards EPA must meet. Focuses on scope, timing, evidence, environmental justice, endangered species, and tribal consultation requirements for rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect state and tribal primacy under the Clean Water Act/Section 401
rubrics_metrics.description: States and tribes have the primary responsibilities and rights to prevent, reduce, and eliminate pollution; Section 401 assures that federal licensing or permitting agencies cannot override state water quality requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite 33 U.S.C. §1251(b), §1313, §1342(b), §1370 and case law (S.D. Warren Co. v. Maine Bd. of Envtl. Prot., PUD No. 1, Sierra Club v. U.S. Army Corps). The Proposed Rule must not usurp or curtail this authority. Anti-patterns: any regulation that narrows state/tribal ability to impose conditions or to deny certifications in a way that allows federal permits to override local water quality standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not narrow the permissible scope of Section 401(d) to discharges only (permit conditions may target the applicant/activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 401(d) authorizes states/tribes to impose limitations on the 'applicant,' not merely on specific 'discharges,' permitting conditions unrelated to the discharge that triggered Section 401 (e.g., minimum instream flow requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on PUD No. 1 of Jefferson County (511 U.S. 700) which held limitations may address applicant conduct broadly. EPA cannot reinterpret 401(d) to coextensively limit scope with 401(a)(1). Anti-patterns: interpreting 'applicant' as requiring conditions tied only to point-source discharges; invoking Brand X/BrandX-style reversal without showing Chevron-appropriate ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize 'discharge' broadly — do not confine Section 401 to point-source discharges
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'discharge' in the Clean Water Act means a 'flowing or issuing out' and is not limited to point sources; non-point-source impacts and activities that alter flows, sediment, temperature, groundwater, etc., may trigger Section 401 review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite S.D. Warren (broad definition), AES Sparrows Point (4th Cir.), and distinguish Ninth Circuit holdings when necessary. EPA must not reinterpret 'discharge' to point-source-only. Examples of non-point impacts: sediment increases, reduced instream flows, thermal loading, destabilized banks, altered groundwater, acid mine drainage, tailings leachate, long-term water-treatment obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking must be justified by an adequate administrative record showing a real problem and that the rule remedies it
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must demonstrate that a problem exists across the universe of Section 401 applications (not just a few 'high-profile' fossil fuel cases) and show that the Proposed Rule will protect water quality or is otherwise justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide data and analysis across project types (thousands of permits per year). Avoid relying only on a handful of denials or anecdotal cases. Anti-patterns: adopting sweeping revisions based on selective examples, failing to show causal link between current rules and alleged detrimental effects, or failing to justify that the proposed changes will be at least equally protective of water quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze impacts across all project types and cumulative regulatory interactions (including other rule changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must evaluate how the Proposed Rule will affect non-fossil-fuel projects (mining, hydroelectric, municipal projects, etc.) and assess interactions with other rulemakings (e.g., revised definition of 'waters of the United States').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include quantitative and qualitative assessment of effects on the thousands of annual certifications beyond Corps/FERC/NRC examples. Perform cumulative impact analysis and account for how other concurrent changes to the Clean Water Act regime will alter Section 401 administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: provide reasonable review timeframes that reflect review realities and complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Arbitrarily short deadlines for Section 401 decisions will prevent states/tribes from determining applicant compliance or developing appropriate conditions and will cause denials or delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many applications are complex, may rely on additional studies, and that delays often stem from 'incomplete requests.' Timeframes should account for applicant and agency pre-filing work, supplemental information, and the need for follow-up. Anti-patterns: rigid short deadlines that do not consider project complexity or supplemental information needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized agencies must be able to request additional information without arbitrary limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Certifying authorities (states, tribes, and EPA when acting as certifier) need flexibility to make follow-up requests as gaps are identified during application review; restricting the number/scope/timing of such requests is arbitrary and undermines review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite FERC practice (pre-filing followed by many additional information requests). Do not adopt rules that foreclose necessary follow-up queries. Consider that EPA's proposed narrow 'certification request' definition would worsen the problem by limiting information provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: States/tribes must retain authority to impose conditions addressing whole-activity impacts (mining, dams, pipelines, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Section 401, states/tribes should be able to condition federal permits to address impacts beyond direct fill discharges — e.g., hydrology changes, sediment storage/resuspension at dams, mine dewatering, tailings seepage, perpetual treatment needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples (hard rock mines, Conowingo Dam, hydroelectric projects) to justify broad conditioning authority. Conditions should be allowed to ensure compliance with state water quality standards and to protect against long-term and indirect harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent federal permitting agencies from second-guessing or overruling state/tribal Section 401 decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Circuit precedent holds that federal agencies lack authority to override or second-guess state/tribal Section 401 determinations; the Proposed Rule's grant of de facto overruling power is unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Sierra Club v. U.S. Army Corps (4th Cir.) and other authority holding federal agencies cannot substitute their judgment for state determinations. Anti-patterns: creating mechanisms or burdens that functionally allow federal permits to evade state-imposed conditions or denials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply any regulatory changes prospectively only; avoid retroactive application
rubrics_metrics.description: If any part of the Proposed Rule takes effect, it should be explicitly prospective and apply only to new applications to avoid regulatory chaos and unfair retroactive effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State that retroactive application would be 'deeply inappropriate' and could cause a 'regulatory nightmare.' Include instruction to clarify prospective-only implementation in the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comply with the Endangered Species Act's consultation requirements before finalizing the rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 7 of the ESA requires federal agencies to consult with USFWS and NMFS to ensure actions will not jeopardize listed species or adversely modify critical habitat; EPA must consult regarding the Proposed Rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how restricting state/tribal conditions could harm listed species by removing protections (e.g., instream flows, sediment control). EPA must avoid irreversible commitments of resources that foreclose measures needed to avoid jeopardy and complete Section 7 consultation prior to final rule adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct a meaningful Environmental Justice analysis consistent with EO 12898 and EPA guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must identify and address disproportionately high and adverse human health or environmental effects of the Proposed Rule on minority, low-income, and indigenous populations, and cannot dismiss potential EJ impacts without support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow EPA's EJ 2020 Action Agenda and EPA EJ Guidance for rulemaking; assessments can be qualitative or quantitative and should begin by understanding the purpose and necessity of the action. Anti-patterns: conclusory statements that the rule has no EJ impacts without analysis; failure to engage affected communities or to address exacerbation of existing disproportionate impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in meaningful government-to-government tribal consultation (EO 13175) and assess effects on tribal waters
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must provide timely, accountable consultation with tribes on policies that have tribal implications, consider disparities in tribal water quality standards and TAS status, and assess how the Proposed Rule would affect tribal waters and enforcement tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consultations occur before final decisions and genuinely consider tribal input. Examples of inadequate practice include scheduling few regional listening sessions and treating tribal inquiries as mere public comments. Account for the fact that many tribes lack NPDES authority and rely heavily on Section 401 authority for protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate pre-filing processes into review timelines and assess applicant commitments made during pre-filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a meaningful pre-filing process exists, the certifying federal agency should consider pre-filing materials, planned post-filing submissions, and whether the applicant failed to provide materials it agreed to submit when determining a 'reasonable' review period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that pre-filing does not eliminate the need for post-filing information requests (FERC example). Timing determinations should reflect pre-filing outcomes and anticipated completion dates rather than imposing inflexible deadlines that ignore agreed-upon supplemental materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and regulatory impact analyses must be complete and not selectively rely on anecdotal high-profile cases
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's Economic Analysis must accurately characterize how often denials occur, causes of delays (e.g., incomplete requests), and whether the Proposed Rule would in fact expedite projects or harm water quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cherry-picking a few fossil fuel infrastructure examples to justify broad rule changes. Provide full accounting of the frequency and outcomes of certifications (thousands annually), and separately analyze impacts on non-fossil-fuel projects and public health/environmental costs.
